title: Chapter 105: Hensheng: To Hate Life 8
content:
Chapter 105

Hensheng: To Hate Life 8

Lan Xichen's voice was tight. "Jin-zongzhu... mind explaining what went on here?"

Jin Guangyao kept his lips sealed, his knuckles whitening as he clenched his fists.

"Looks like our Chief Cultivator isn't feeling chatty," Wei Wuxian said lightly.

Flicking his wrist, a naked female corpse materialized right beneath his hand. Wei Wuxian rested his palm flat against the scorched, blackened crown of her skull. "Lucky for me, your silence doesn't mean I can't find out."

The moment Empathy took hold, before his eyes could even adjust to the light, Wei Wuxian was overwhelmed by a suffocating cloud of cheap cosmetic powder.

A high, saccharine giggle spilled right out of his own mouth: "...Her? Oh, she wanted out bad. She was already in her late twenties when she hooked up with him—practically over the hill in this line of work. A couple more years and no one would've touched her with a ten-foot pole. That's why she took all those beatings and insisted on popping out a son. Thought it was her ticket out of the gutter. But hey, it takes two to tango, doesn't it?"

His vision cleared.

He was sitting inside a sprawling, garishly decorated parlor lined with over a dozen banquet tables. Each was packed with drunken patrons and working girls in various stages of undress—some baring porcelain shoulders, some with loose, tumbled updos, some perched right on men's laps giggling into wine cups. The whole room reeked of spilled liquor and cheap perfume.

It didn't take a genius to figure out what kind of establishment this was.

So the ones burned alive under this temple were brothel workers, Wei Wuxian realized. No wonder those spirits were stark naked. Prostitutes and their clients.

A patron beside her took a swig and grinned. "Blood's blood, isn't it? The guy really just walked away from his own kid?"

"Well, according to her, the father was some grand lord from a legendary cultivating clan," she scoffed, pouring another cup. "A guy like that probably has half a dozen sons running around Koi Tower already. When you've got that much gold and seed, what's one little bastard in the gutter? She spent fourteen years holding her breath, waiting for her white knight to scoop her up. Never came, did he? Had to feed the brat all on her own."

The table chuckled, trading cynical looks. "A grand cultivator? Pull the other one. She actually expect people to buy that?"

"Aiya, what reason do I have to lie to you fine gentlemen?" she simpered, swaying her hips as she spotted a lanky teenage boy carrying a heavy tea tray across the parlor. She snapped her fingers: "Xiao Meng! Get over here!"

The boy dutifully shuffled over, keeping his eyes pinned politely to the floorboards. "Sister Anxin, did you need something?"

In an instant, everything clicked into place in Wei Wuxian's head.

The drunkards leaned back, raking Meng Yao with disdainful, mocking eyes.

Meng Yao held the wooden tray steady, murmuring, "Was there something you needed me to fetch?"

Anxin smirked, resting her chin on her hand. "Say, Xiao Meng, are you still keeping up with your little studies?"

Meng Yao blinked, looking lost. "My... studies?"

"You know, all those fancy gentleman hobbies your dear mother forces on you! Calligraphy, court etiquette, swordplay, meditation chants... how's the grand heir doing with his lessons?"

Snorts and smothered laughter broke out around the table.

Anxin playfully shushed the men, leaning across the wood: "Don't laugh, I'm entirely serious! His mother raises him like he's a young lord from an ancient sect. Teaches him to read, buys stacks of bogus cultivation manuals off street vendors, and even paid a pretty penny to ship him off to private school!"

One of the customers nearly choked on his peanut. "School? A whore's kid in a real academy? You're pulling my leg."

"Not a word of a lie!" Anxin crowed. "Xiao Meng, tell these nice masters. You went to the local academy, didn't you?"

A patron raised a brow. "He still going?"

"Quit after three days," Anxin said, rolling her eyes. "Came scuttling right back and threw a fit, refusing to step foot outside ever since. Tell us, Xiao Meng: do you hate reading, or did the other kids not want to play with the brothel boy?"

Meng Yao didn't say a word.

Anxin burst into giggles, reaching out with a long, crimson-tipped nail to jab him hard right between the brows. "What's with the long face, little guy? Did big sister hurt your feelings?"

She drove her fingernail in deep, leaving a sharp, bright-red indent right at the center of his forehead—an uncanny, twisted echo of a noble vermilion mark.

Meng Yao slowly raised a sleeve, brushing his fingers over the bruised spot. "No..."

"Alright, shoo," Anxin waved him off with a flick of her wrist. "Back to work with you."

Meng Yao turned on his heel to walk away, but before he took three paces, she plucked a green plum from the ceramic dish on the table and pitched it at his back. "Here! A little treat for your hard work."

Meng Yao looked back just in time for the unripe fruit to crack hard against his ribs. It dropped with a hollow thud, rolling away across the dusty floor.

Anxin clucked her tongue. "Useless thing. Can't even catch a plum. Pick it up, don't let it go to waste!"

A small smile tugged at the corner of Meng Yao’s mouth. He was supposed to be fourteen, but his malnourished frame made him look barely twelve. Seeing that delicate, polite smile stretch across his childish face sent a cold, greasy shiver down Wei Wuxian's spine.

The boy bent down, scooped the bruised fruit out of the dirt, and wiped it clean against his cheap hemp tunic. The smile on his face widened, smooth and practiced: "Thank you, Sister Anxin."

"Don't mention it," she said with an airy wave. "Scram."

"Call if you need anything else," he murmured, slipping into the crowd.

Watching him walk away, one of the men shook his head. "If I had a son living in a pit like this, I'd move heaven and earth to buy him out."

"Is the father really a highborn cultivator?" another mused. "Ransoming a girl and tossing a few coppers for child support is pocket change to those guys. Less than an afternoon's work."

Anxin spat a watermelon seed onto the floor. "And you believe her? If a woman like that tells you the sky is blue, you'd better check for rain. A 'grand lord'? That's just her trying to pretty up her shame. In reality, it was probably some tacky traveling merchant with loose change, and she blew it up into an epic love story—"

A woman’s blood-curdling shriek shattered the chatter.

From the second-floor gallery came the violent clatter of shattering porcelain. A heavy rosewood zither tumbled through the balustrade, smashing into kindling right in the center of the first-floor parlor with a concussive crack. Splintered wood and snapped silk strings flew everywhere, drawing a barrage of curses from nearby patrons who scrambled out of the way.

Anxin jumped out of her skin, screeching, "What in heaven's name?!"

Across the hall, Meng Yao’s face drained of color. "Mother!"

Up on the gallery, a burly customer was dragging a woman by her hair, hauling her bodily out of a private suite. Anxin grabbed her patron's arm, her voice buzzing with malicious excitement: "Look, look! She's getting what's coming to her again!"

Meng Yao scrambled up the stairs. The woman was clutching her aching scalp with one hand, frantically using the other to yank her torn robes over her bare shoulders. Spotting the boy sprinting up, she gasped, "I told you to stay downstairs! Go back! Get down there right now!"

Meng Yao lunged forward, clawing desperately at the man's iron wrists. The brute didn't even blink—he drove a heavy leather boot straight into the kid's stomach.

Meng Yao bounced down the entire flight of wooden stairs, tumbling head over heels with sickening thuds, drawing terrified gasps from the crowd below.

Wei Wuxian’s gut twisted.

This was the third time he’d seen this man kicked down a flight of stairs.

The woman let out a broken, agonizing scream, but the man merely dragged her down by her dark hair, tearing the remnants of her silk robes until she was practically bare. He shoved her violently through the front entrance, sending her crashing onto the muddy street. Spitting a thick glob of phlegm right onto her bare skin, he barked, "Ugly, stuck-up hag! An old whore thinking she's still a fresh virgin!"

The woman huddled in the muck, shaking uncontrollably, terrified to lift her head because the slightest shift would expose her fully to the street. Passersby halted in their tracks, caught between faux-shock and perverted thrill, whispering, pointing, their eyes raking hungrily over her shivering skin.

Inside, the parlor girls crowded around the doorway, giggling behind their sleeves like Anxin, eagerly breaking down the drama for their leering clients.

Just then, a young courtesan pushed her way past the gossiping flock. She untied her flimsy outer wrap on the move, leaving her full, porcelain chest loosely bound in a scarlet undergarment, her impossibly narrow waist catching the eyes of every man on the block. The street fell dead silent, the crowd turning to gawk at her instead.

The girl spat venomously into the dirt. "Look at what, you pack of dogs?! What're you staring at your mother for?! Think looking at me is free?! Staring costs money! Pay up! Cough up the silver, you cheap bastards!"

She actually lunged forward, thrusting her palms right into the faces of the onlookers, barking at them to pay.

The shameless shouting scattered the crowd in a hurry. Rolling her eyes, the girl tossed her sheer robe over the weeping woman, hauling her to her feet and steering her back into the parlor. As they stumbled inside, she scolded without mercy: "I told you to quit this ridiculous act! Who are you playing the virtuous lady for in a place like this? See what you get? Learn your damn lesson!"

Wei Wuxian’s eyes narrowed as he watched her profile. Why does this woman look so familiar? Where have I seen her before?

The fallen woman wept softly, clutching her bruised collar. "A-Yao... A-Yao..."

Meng Yao had taken that kick so hard he was still dry-heaving on the floorboards, struggling to find his footing. The bold girl hauled the boy up by his arm, dragging both mother and son toward the back quarters.

At Anxin’s table, one of the patrons leaned in, his eyes tracking her swaying hips. "Who was that firecracker?"

Anxin cracked a sunflower seed between her teeth, unimpressed. "A foul-tempered shrew. You stay far away from that one."

Another customer sighed, shaking his head. "So that was Meng Shi? The famous poetic courtesan from back in the day? Look what she's been reduced to."

Anxin flashed another syrupy, disdainful grin. "That's what happens when you're an idiot. Insisting on keeping a brat—once a woman pops out a kid, her figure is ruined. If she wasn't clinging to that pathetic 'poetic genius' reputation from ten years ago, nobody would even pay her a copper. If you ask me, all that book-learning fried her brains."

"Can't argue with that," the patron agreed with a laugh. "Girls who touch too many books always carry that ridiculous, high-and-mighty chip on their shoulder. Can't let go of their silly little daydreams."

"If she could feed herself by writing poetry, I'd shut my mouth," Anxin scoffed. "It’s just a cheap parlor trick to lure in customers anyway! Let's be real here—we're all selling the same skin. You read a couple of scrolls, and suddenly you're higher than the rest of us? Who do you think you're looking down on? The customers think she's a joke, and none of the girls can stand her. Men come to a place like this to watch a timid sixteen-year-old play coy for a little novelty. Who wants to pay good silver to watch an old hag play hard to get? Her ship sailed years ago! Everyone knows it—she’s the only idiot who refuses to wake up—"

A hand tapped Anxin sharply on the shoulder.

She spun around—and took a crackling, bare-palm slap straight across the jaw.

Smack!

The force rattled her teeth. Anxin sat stunned for a second before screeching like a banshee: "You miserable slut!"

The bold courtesan glared down at her, chest heaving. "Slut yourself! If you've got so much energy to flap your gums, go use that tongue to service another customer!"

"What I say is none of your damn business!"

The two women threw themselves at each other, tumbling onto the parlor floor in a flurry of tearing nails, gnashing teeth, and flying hairpins. Foul curses flew like spit—promising to carve up faces, sneering that the other couldn't even pay men to bed her. The patrons quickly jumped in to drag them apart, yelling, "Sisi! Let go! Stop fighting!"

Sisi?!

A cold jolt ran down Wei Wuxian’s spine.

He finally knew why the face had scratched at his memory. Add half a dozen faded, jagged knife scars across those smooth cheeks, and she was the spitting image of the scarred courtesan who had just blown Jin Guangyao's secrets wide open at Lotus Pier!

Before he could process the thought, a wave of blistering, suffocating heat washed over the room.

The entire parlor was swallowed in a raging sea of crimson fire.

Wei Wuxian yanked himself violently out of the spiritual link!

He snapped his eyes open.

Lan Wangji’s pale gaze found him instantly. "Okay?"

Lan Xichen stepped closer. "Master Wei, what did you see?"

Wei Wuxian took a long, steadying breath, shaking the smell of smoke and cosmetic powder from his senses. "I'm guessing this Guanyin Temple was built right over the building Jin-zongzhu grew up in."

Jin Guangyao didn't flinch.

Jiang Cheng frowned. "Where he grew up? Didn't he grow up in a..." He caught himself before spitting the vulgar word, his eyes widening as the pieces fell into place. "This was the brothel! He set the whole damn block on fire, burned it to ash, and paved a temple right over it!"

Lan Xichen looked at Jin Guangyao, his voice quiet. "Did you light that match?"

Jin Guangyao’s voice was disturbingly flat. "I did."

Jiang Cheng scoffed. "Look at you, owning up to your crimes without a fight for once."

"Given where we're standing," Jin Guangyao murmured, "does one more sin make a difference?"

Lan Xichen fell silent for a long moment. "...Was it to wipe your trail clean?"

Everyone in the cultivation realm knew Lianfang-zun had clawed his way out of the gutter, but in all these years, not a single soul had been able to pin down the exact establishment he hailed from. It was an open secret that Jin Guangyao had systematically scrubbed his past from the historical record, but nobody had imagined he’d simply burned the entire place to the ground, leaving no living witnesses behind.

"Not entirely," Jin Guangyao replied softly.

Lan Xichen let out a hollow sigh, turning his face away.

Jin Guangyao watched him. "Aren't you going to ask me why?"

Lan Xichen gave a tired shake of his head. "In the past, it wasn't that I was blind to your actions. I simply chose to believe you were forced into corners, that you had your reasons." He paused, the disappointment bleeding raw in his tone: "But you have gone far beyond reason. And I... no longer know what to believe."

Outside, the storm howled like a wounded beast, the wind whistling shrilly through the cracks in the barred wooden doors. In the middle of that eerie, lonely wail, Jin Guangyao dropped to his knees with a dull thud.

The entire hall froze.

Even Wei Wuxian, who was casually tucking the soft sword he’d confiscated into his own sash, blinked in pure bewilderment.

Jin Guangyao’s voice trembled, utterly drained: "Er-ge. I was wrong."

Wei Wuxian felt second-hand embarrassment crawling up his neck. He couldn't resist a dry cough: "Look, if you have something to say, can we just throw down with fists instead? Let's stick to violence, yeah?"

The man's pride was entirely fluid—flipping his face like a mask, dropping to his knees without a scrap of dignity, completely shameless.

Lan Xichen’s expression was agonizing to behold.

Jin Guangyao pressed on, looking up with raw, pleading eyes: "Er-ge, we've walked side by side for so many years. Whatever else I've done, you know how I've treated you. I have zero interest in the seat of Chief Cultivator anymore. The Yin Tiger Tally is entirely ruined. Once tonight is over, I’m boarding a vessel for the Eastern Seas, never to set foot on these shores again. For the sake of our past... please, give me a way out."

The Eastern Seas. To put it plainly: he was fleeing into exile.

It sounded humiliating, but Jin Guangyao had always been famous for bending like a reed rather than snapping like an oak; if bowing his head kept him breathing, he’d kiss the dirt. The Lanling Jin Clan could crush three or four prominent houses with sheer military might, but if every clan in the realm formed a coalition against him, falling like the Wen Clan of Qishan was only a matter of time. Fleeing into the unknown to preserve his strength was a calculated gamble—survive today, and who was to say he wouldn't build a new army tomorrow?

Wei Wuxian tilted his head. "Jin-zongzhu, you claim the Yin Tiger Tally is broken. Mind whipping it out so I can take a look?"

Jin Guangyao met his gaze evenly. "Master Wei, a replica is only a replica. Its durability had a hard limit, and the tally burned out completely. Besides, nobody knows the sheer, volatile toxicity of that artifact better than the man who forged it. An empty husk that can no longer command corpses, bringing nothing but bloody retribution to whoever holds it—do you truly believe I'd keep that kind of liability on my person?"

Wei Wuxian chuckled. "Who knows? Maybe you've got another Xue Yang tucked away somewhere."

"Er-ge," Jin Guangyao turned back to Lan Xichen, his voice breaking with earnest devotion, "every word I speak is the truth."

He laid the sincerity on thick, and looking back, he really had treated Lan Xichen with spotless courtesy throughout the entire ordeal. Lan Xichen couldn't bring himself to turn completely cold, but his voice was heavy with exhaustion: "Jin-zongzhu. The moment you chose to orchestrate that slaughter on the Burial Mounds, I told you: you do not get to call me 'Er-ge' ever again."

"The Burial Mounds was a catastrophic misstep," Jin Guangyao admitted softly, lowering his head. "I lost my head. But... I had no road left to walk."

Lan Xichen frowned. "What do you mean, no road left?"

Lan Wangji’s voice was pure, biting frost: "Brother. Do not engage."

Wei Wuxian jumped in to back him: "Lan-zongzhu, remember what you warned Jiang-zongzhu earlier? Don't let him start talking."

Lan Xichen knew better than anyone how venomously persuasive Jin Guangyao's silver tongue could be. Yet the moment the hint of an untold secret was dangled before him, he couldn't stop himself from listening.

Jin Guangyao locked onto that hesitation like a hawk.

He lowered his voice to a whisper:

"I received a letter."
